newsitem.title: DUBAI: Oman investors flock to take up new share issues.
newsitem.headline: Oman investors flock to take up new share issues.

text.p: Heavy oversubscription to initial public offerings in Oman highlights the widespread belief among local investors that the issues promise large profits in a very short time, analysts said on Wednesday.
It also shows revived confidence in the Gulf's most open market, coupled with high domestic liquidity and faith in the strength of the banking system, they said.
Alliance Housing Bank, the latest of 12 initial public offerings on the Muscat stock exchange so far this year, attracted demand for 96 times more shares than the eight million on offer.

"People are crazy, they expect Alliance to go the same way as other issues like Oman Savings and Finance Bank which is up at 2.70 rials from 1.02 at issue only months ago," said one stock watcher by telephone from Muscat.
"This is not a record subscription only for Oman but a record in the region," Muscat Securities Market executive president Mahmoud al-Jarwani said.
He said all 12 IPOs so far in 1997 were oversubscribed.
Alliance issue manager and lead promoter Mohamed Habib said investors applied for 787.9 million rials ($2.09 billion) worth of shares.
"It is amazing. This means we can only give people 1.1 percent of what they requested," he told Reuters.
The bank, which will be the first private specialist housing bank in Oman, offered the public eight million shares at one rial each, or 1.02 rials including a fee for issue expenses.

"One major factor is the people's confidence in the growth of Oman's economy. They have confidence in Oman's rules and what they see as good performance in the capital market. Oman is gradually opening up to foreign investors and liquidity is available in the country," Jarwani said.
The 105 issues listed on the eight-year-old market are capitalised at around $5 billion. So far this year the market index has climbed more than 40 percent after 1996's 30 percent jump.
"There is a need for housing loans as Oman's population is growing at more than 3.5 percent. So there is good potential for the bank to give a good return on investment," Jarwani added.
"People believe a bank is a safe investment because of strict central bank regulation and the fact that the country would never allow a bank to fail," Habib said.

He said Alliance's appeal also had to do with the fact that the state's housing bank had a six-year waiting list and only one other bank offered mortgages in a country where some 60 percent of the population was under 18.
Habib added that among subscribers were two British fund managers which had applied for $30 million in Alliance shares.
Relatively low-volume trade in the past few weeks on the bourse was due to interest in the Alliance issue, analysts said.
"The market has been weak because people have been saving up their last pennies to subscribe to Alliance," said one broker.
Others said investors had taken bank loans to finance share purchases. But as they would get only a portion of applications, there was concern they would be unable to pay the interest.
"The Central Bank warned banks not to give the loans as many small investors do not know the risks," said one analyst.
Bankers confirmed they had received instruction from the Central Bank not to give loans specifically to invest in IPOs.
Despite the small share allotments and the loan clamp down, analysts said investors were unlikely to be deterred.
"We are going to be very busy this year. I expect around 20 to 25 new issues coming to the market this year. Our market is greedy for more," Jarwani said.
